A16-8.label: Existentialist Film
A16-8.defn: An art-film character study whose engine is a crisis of meaning in the present tense — alienation, ennui, or a self disguised or doubled (La Dolce Vita, The Silence, Lost in Translation, The Passenger, The Double Life of Véronique). A life weighed up at its middle or end goes to the Midlife Crisis Film; a clinical inner state to A16-7; a quiet everyday portrait to A16-9.
A16-8.axis: by the shape of the crisis: alienation first, divided by era (the postwar modernist wave to 1979, its late-modernist continuation in the 1980s–90s, the contemporary festival film), then the ennui of the affluent, and double lives and masks last

new_leaves.label: Midlife Crisis Film
new_leaves.breadth: existential dramas of a life weighed up — at its middle, in old age, or reviewed whole from rise to fall
new_leaves.defn: A drama whose crisis of meaning comes from taking stock of a life already lived: the midlife crisis, the reckoning of old age, or a whole life reviewed in its rise and fall (Dodsworth, Save the Tiger, Husbands, Citizen Kane, Death of a Salesman, Youth, Gran Torino). Test: the film's engine is the review of a life's course rather than a present-tense alienation (A16-8) or a clinical breakdown (A16-7).
new_leaves.aliases: midlife-crisis drama; late-life drama; life-review film
new_leaves.axis: by where the life is weighed up: the whole life reviewed in its rise and fall first, then the crisis at midlife, and old age and last reckonings last

A16-22.label: Social Problem Film
A16-22.defn: A drama built to expose one named social ill of prejudice, violence or patriarchy — racism and caste, youth violence and its institutions, sexual violence and reproductive rights, the oppression of women (Gentleman's Agreement, Within Our Gates, Never Rarely Sometimes Always, Moolaadé). Addiction goes to the Addiction Drama; prostitution and trafficking to the Prostitution Film; diffuse working-class hardship to A16-19; the courtroom to A16-25.
A16-22.axis: by the social ill: race and caste first, then youth violence and reform schools, sexual violence and reproductive rights, and the oppression of women last

new_leaves.label: Addiction Drama
new_leaves.breadth: social-problem dramas of drink, drugs and gambling
new_leaves.defn: A drama whose engine is one person's or one milieu's addiction — to alcohol, drugs or gambling — followed through craving, collapse and (sometimes) recovery (The Lost Weekend, Days of Wine and Roses, The Man with the Golden Arm, Requiem for a Dream, The Gambler). Test: the addiction itself is the subject, not a backdrop to crime (A2) or a psychological portrait (A16-7).
new_leaves.aliases: drug film; alcoholism film; addiction film
new_leaves.axis: by the substance: drink first, then drugs, and gambling last

new_leaves.label: Prostitution Film
new_leaves.breadth: dramas of sex work, the fallen woman and trafficking
new_leaves.defn: A drama whose subject is prostitution as a social condition — the fallen woman of the silent and studio eras, the brothel and the red-light district, the street, and modern trafficking (Diary of a Lost Girl, Street of Shame, Nights of Cabiria, Mamma Roma, Lilya 4-Ever, Much Loved). Test: selling sex is the protagonist's situation and the film's subject; an erotic treatment goes to A15.
new_leaves.aliases: fallen-woman film; sex-work drama; trafficking drama
new_leaves.axis: by era, as the field divides it: the fallen-woman film of the silent and early sound eras, the postwar brothel and red-light film, then the modern sex-work and trafficking drama

A19-5.label: Diary Film
A19-5.defn: A first-person documentary whose subject is the filmmaker's own life as it is lived and recorded — the film diary, the home movie, the video or digital self-portrait, the chronicle of illness, exile or confinement (Reminiscences of a Journey to Lithuania, Sherman's March, Tarnation, Dear Diary, This Is Not a Film). A film that turns the camera on the filmmaker's parents, siblings or family history goes to the Family Documentary.
A19-5.axis: by the diary's form and occasion: home movies first, the New American Cinema film diary and the essayistic life-diary, auteurs' diaries and self-portraits, then diaries of illness, exile and political confinement, and the video and digital diary last
secs: Film Diaries of the New American Cinema & After

new_leaves.label: Family Documentary (Domestic Ethnography)
new_leaves.breadth: first-person documentaries about the filmmaker's own family
new_leaves.defn: A first-person documentary in which the filmmaker turns the camera on their own family — a parent, grandparent, sibling or child, or a family secret and history — and the film is about them rather than the filmmaker's own days (Sink or Swim, Nobody's Business, Stories We Tell, Dick Johnson Is Dead, The Flat, No Home Movie). Test: the family member or family past is the subject; the filmmaker's own life chronicled stays in the Diary Film.
new_leaves.aliases: domestic ethnography; family portrait documentary; autobiographical family documentary
new_leaves.axis: by whom the camera turns to: parents and grandparents first, then siblings, children and the household, and family secrets and histories last

A16-6.label: Melodrama
A16-6.defn: A drama in the melodramatic mode — heightened emotion, sacrifice and fate carried by music and mise-en-scène — whose sacrifice is made for a child or a family, or to illness (Stella Dallas, Imitation of Life, Written on the Wind, Dark Victory, All About My Mother). The melodrama of the fallen, desiring or self-sacrificing woman in love goes to the Woman's Film; realist family dramas to A16-3 to A16-5.
A16-6.axis: by the sacrifice at the core: maternal sacrifice first, then the family melodrama, the illness tearjerker, and Sirk's non-melodrama studio pictures last

new_leaves.label: Woman's Film
new_leaves.breadth: melodramas of the fallen, desiring or self-sacrificing woman, across national studio traditions
new_leaves.defn: A melodrama centred on a woman's desire, fall or sacrifice in love, marriage or work, made for and around a female star or a woman's point of view (The Cheat, Pandora's Box, Back Street, All That Heaven Allows, When a Woman Ascends the Stairs, Far from Heaven). Test: the heroine's own passion or fall is the engine; sacrifice for a child or a family stays in A16-6.
new_leaves.aliases: woman's picture; women's film; fallen-woman melodrama; josei eiga
new_leaves.axis: by era and national studio tradition: the silent vamp and fallen woman first, then the Hollywood woman's film, the European, Japanese, Chinese-Korean-Indian and Latin American traditions, and the modern revisionist woman's film last
